summary:
We built PULSAR, a visual self-assessment app for astronauts on long missions. Crew members log their health readings and get a clear status (nominal, caution or critical) for each reading, each body system on an interactive body map, and themselves as a whole. Trend alerts give early warning when a value is still in range but drifting from that person’s own 7-day baseline. Each mission setting (space station, deep-space transit, lunar base, Mars base, rover) has its own communication delay, medical support and plan for when to call the ground.

PULSAR is built from NASA’s own documents. It schedules the checks NASA requires for each mission day and explains each one in plain words. It also shows findings from NASA’s Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health program, such as how cabin CO₂ levels relate to headaches. Dr. Jarvis, an AI assistant running on MedGemma, answers health questions using the astronaut’s own readings and cites NASA Human Research Program sources. PULSAR works offline and produces a 7-day report for the flight surgeon.

This matters because on a Mars mission a message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way. Crews will need to judge their own health, catch problems early and know what to do next without waiting for help from the ground.
details:
PULSAR: Crew Health Monitor

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Health Monitoring Software challenge. Live at https://pulsar-health.pages.dev

1. Problem

  • Astronauts on the Space Station can reach the ground right away: a flight surgeon sees their data and answers in seconds.
  • On missions to the Moon and Mars, that link breaks. A message from Mars can take up to 22 minutes each way, and the crew can lose contact entirely.
  • NASA's Human Research Program names five hazards of deep space: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a closed environment. Together they affect every body system: bones, muscles, heart, eyes, sleep and mood.
  • Early warning signs are small and easy to miss. NASA's astronaut health data (LSAH, its Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health program) found that each 1 mmHg rise in cabin CO₂ almost doubles the odds of a headache.
  • Health tools often assume a male body by default. As crews include more women, a tool that ignores female biology can miss real problems, or flag normal changes as problems.
  • The core question: when Earth can't answer, who does the crew ask?

2. Solution

PULSAR is a crew health monitor that works on its own, offline, while the crew waits for the ground. One look answers three questions: How am I? What changed? What do I do now?

  • Readings go through a rules engine based on NASA ranges. The result is a clear status: nominal, caution or critical.
  • A personal 7-day baseline catches slow drifts while a value is still in its normal range.
  • Built for every crew member: the body model, the trend checks and the AI assistant adapt to female and male astronauts.
  • Dr. Jarvis, an AI assistant running on MedGemma, answers questions using the astronaut's own readings and NASA's research, and cites its sources.
  • Report to ground sends the flight surgeon a 7-day summary. A live countdown shows when it will reach Earth. Until the reply arrives, the app tells the crew what to do on board.

3. Features

  • Status first: one overall status (nominal, caution or critical), always written out in words as well as shown in color.
  • Interactive 3D body: a full anatomical model with skin, muscles, bones, blood vessels and organs. The heart beats, the lungs breathe, and critical systems pulse. Tap a system to see its readings, the hazard behind it, and guidance.
  • Logging readings: one tap from anywhere, with "how to measure" help, a live status preview as you type, input checks, and Undo on every change.
    • Body model: female crew get a 3D body that includes the female reproductive organs. Everyone gets the same detailed model and the same layers.
    • Menstrual cycle tracking (optional): a "Your cycle" card shows the current phase, when the next period is due (with a range of days), and an estimate of ovulation. It learns cycle length from logged periods and widens its estimates for irregular cycles. It also covers hormonal contraception and period suppression (pill, continuous pill, IUD, implant, injection), which many astronauts use in flight.
    • Fewer false alarms: after ovulation, body temperature normally rises about 0.4 °C and resting heart rate about 3 bpm. PULSAR allows for this in its trend checks, so a normal cycle isn't flagged as a warning, but a real fever still is.
    • Dr. Jarvis takes it into account: the assistant knows the astronaut's sex and cycle phase, so its answers fit their body.
    • Two demo profiles, female and male, so judges can see both.
  • Mission environments: space station, deep-space transit, lunar base, Mars base and rover. Each has its own communication delay, medical support, escalation plan and adjusted thresholds.
    • NASA's required checks scheduled by flight day: medical and family calls, fitness tests, eye and hearing tests, body mass and more
    • 44 NASA requirements across 10 body systems, each explained in plain words: what is measured, why, when, and how to prepare
    • 21 research findings with their numbers
    • The yearly lifetime exam and the history of the LSAH program
  • Field manual: what each status means, the five hazards, a reference for every indicator, and the escalation plan.
  • Gamification: XP, levels, streaks and badges that reward logging consistently, never "good" values.
  • Report to ground: a 7-day summary for the flight surgeon that includes the astronaut's sex, as copied text, Markdown or JSON.
  • Works offline: an installable app (PWA) that runs on phone, tablet or laptop and keeps all data on the device.

4. Inputs

What the crew logs:

Body system

Indicators

Main hazard

Brain & behavior

Sleep hours, mood (1–5)

Isolation, distance

Immune

Body temperature

Radiation, closed environment

Lungs

SpO₂, cabin CO₂

Closed environment

Heart

Resting heart rate, systolic/diastolic blood pressure

Altered gravity, radiation

Metabolism

Fasting glucose

Altered gravity, nutrition

Bones & muscles

Exercise minutes

Altered gravity

Profile and settings:

  • Crew name, mission start date (day 1), mission environment
  • Sex: female or male
  • Cycle (female crew only, optional): regular, irregular or none; date of the last period; typical cycle and period length; hormonal method, if any

Questions: free text typed to Dr. Jarvis.

Reference data the app is built on:

  • 76 NASA medical requirement documents
  • 10 LSAH newsletters and 15 LSAH paper abstracts
  • 147 NASA and Canadian Space Agency documents for the AI library: about 700,000 words, split into 3,970 passages

What the crew gets back: a status for each reading, each body system and the person overall; guidance; trend warnings that account for the menstrual cycle; cycle predictions; a cited answer from Dr. Jarvis; and the report to ground.

5. Tools and technologies

Area

Technology

Frontend

Vite, React 19, TypeScript

Styling

Tailwind CSS v4 with design tokens; supports reduced motion, reduced transparency and high contrast

3D body

Three.js with React Three Fiber; the female and male models are built with glTF-Transform

Animation

Framer Motion

Charts

Recharts, with normal and caution bands drawn behind each trend

State and storage

Zustand, saved to localStorage, with versioned data migrations

Rules engine

Pure TypeScript with JSON thresholds (no code changes needed to edit them), plus a cycle engine; unit-tested with Vitest

Offline

Hand-written service worker and web app manifest

AI model

MedGemma 1.5 (4B), served by a Python backend

AI search (RAG)

Keyword search (BM25) plus meaning-based search (bge-base-en-v1.5 embeddings), merged by rank fusion, then reranked by a cross-encoder (ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2) that also filters out off-topic questions

Hosting

Cloudflare Pages, a Pages Function at /api/chat, Cloudflare Tunnel and KV for sharing the model

Development

Claude Code, Graphify (code knowledge graph)

6. Why PULSAR? (what's new)

  1. Built on NASA's own science. Thresholds, the flight-day check schedule and 21 research findings come directly from NASA's LSAH program and Human Research Program. Nothing is generic.
  2. Built for distance. Each mission environment has its own communication delay and escalation plan, so the app's advice changes when the ground is 22 minutes away.
  3. Warns early. Comparing each reading to the person's own baseline catches a slow drift days before it becomes a problem, not only after a value is out of range.
  4. Inclusive by design. PULSAR doesn't assume a male body. It adapts its body model, its warnings and its AI answers to female and male astronauts. Its cycle-aware trend checks keep a normal menstrual cycle from being flagged as a health problem.
  5. An AI that cites its sources. Dr. Jarvis answers from 147 NASA documents and links to the exact page, so its answers can be checked.
  6. Builds a habit. Rewards go to logging regularly, never to "good" numbers, because the most useful health data is the data that actually gets logged.
  7. Private and offline. Everything runs on the device, and the AI model can run on the crew's own hardware.

7. Conclusion

The farther we travel, the longer the wait between a question and its answer. PULSAR fills that wait: it turns a crew member who is waiting into one who knows what's happening. It combines NASA's medical science, early-warning trends, a cited AI assistant and an offline design in one simple, status-first app. And it works for every crew member: female or male, PULSAR adapts to the body it monitors. On Mars, help is 22 minutes away. PULSAR is there in the first second.

8. Future work

  • Pre-flight baselines: set each person's baseline from their data on Earth, not only a rolling average during flight.
  • Camera and wearable input: read a device's display from a photo, run skin and eye checks, and import data from wearables.
  • Several crew members on one device: with an overview for the crew medical officer (CMO).
  • More sex-specific health guidance: adjust more ranges for female and male crew, such as blood pressure and glucose, and add NASA's sex-specific findings (for example on eye changes and radiation risk) to the research section.
  • AI on the device itself: run a compressed model directly on the crew's device, with no backend needed.
  • Sync with the ground: two-way data exchange with mission control that tolerates delays.
  • Validation: check the thresholds against official NASA flight rules and test with analog missions such as HERA.

Before you submit, check two things:

  • The "male by default" point in Section 1 is general framing that I added. If the judges may ask for a source, drop that bullet or cite one.
  • Future work: only the first three items are on the README's roadmap. I added the other four, so remove any the team isn't planning.
